    My Personal Sleep Aid “Clinical Trial”

    Getting your  sleep doesn't get easier in the Golden Years

    By
    Robert Kay
    -
    September 28, 2026
    0
    199
    Facebook
    X
    Pinterest
    WhatsApp
      Listen to audio version of this article
      Sponsored by
      0:00 / 12:36
      Instaread

      Got “sleep issues”? Don’t feel alone. According to the American Academy of  Sleep Medicine and the National Institutes of  Health, sleep disorders affect an estimated 50 million to 70 million Americans. While roughly one in five adults has a chronic sleep disorder, nearly half of adults over age 65 experience chronic sleep problems, making poor sleep one of the most common health complaints among older Americans.

      Welcome to my world.

      Sometimes it’s difficult to fall asleep, and I’ll wake up multiple times in the middle of the night.

      I brought it up with my primary care physician during my annual visit. She listened intently, agreed it was common for kupuna, and offered to write a prescription for sleeping pills. I told her no; I wanted to avoid pharmaceuticals if possible.

      At the same time, I needed to do something. I was on a mission to find that silver bullet of a supplement. It had to be out there.

      Right?

      Advertisement

      I had tried CBD/THC concoctions and they worked with one caveat. Using this prevented me from remembering dreams. That’s a no go. I believe dreams are a connection to the unconscious. For me understanding what the unconscious has to say is very important. So although the CBD/THC potions did help with sleep, there was no free lunch.

      Naturally, I went looking online, and before long I was in the algorithm’s target zone. Every conceivable mushroom concoction, melatonin blend, ashwagandha additive—you name it—appeared in my Facebook feed.

      It was dizzying.

      Once again, it was time to seek professional guidance. I called my friend Traci Potterf, a functional medicine specialist and the founder of Inner Genius Health. She suggested Deep Sleep, a melatonin-free herbal sleep supplement.

      Deep Sleep (Herbs, Etc.)

      Deep Sleep is made by Herbs, Etc., a Santa Fe, New Mexico, company founded in 1969. It operates along the lines of a family business, with a philosophy rooted in traditional Western herbal medicine. The National Institutes of Health defines traditional Western herbal medicine as “a form of primary healthcare that utilizes naturally occurring plant materials—such as roots, bark, leaves, and flowers—with minimal industrial processing to treat illness, prevent disease, and promote holistic well-being.”

      That sounded good to me.

      Deep Sleep’s ingredients all come from plants, including valerian root, passionflower, chamomile, lemon balm, California poppy, oat seed, and orange peel. It is the company’s flagship product and the No. 1-selling natural sleep aid in the U.S. natural retail channel—stores that specialize in natural, organic, and health-focused products rather than conventional outlets.

      What distinguishes Herbs, Etc. from many supplement makers is its emphasis on fresh plant extraction. For herbs whose active compounds are thought to be volatile or delicate, the company buys freshly harvested plants rather than relying solely on dried material. Other herbs are used dried when that better preserves their constituents.

      Besides Deep Sleep, the company offers a catalog of 79 herbal remedies. Its categories include Allergy & Respiratory Support (Allertonic® and Respiratonic®), Immune Defense (Phytocillin® and Ultimate Echinacea), Stress & Nervous System Health (Stress ReLeaf®), Vocal Care (Singers Saving Grace®), and Menstrual Comfort (Cramp ReLeaf®).

      The products come in liquid tinctures, softgels, and concentrated gummies.

      I used Deep Sleep as both a softgel and a tincture (more on that later).

      The next sleep aid I chose was magnesium.

      Advertisement

      Magnesium glycinate (Thorne)

      Friends had recommended one magnesium formulation or another, and the press was full of glowing reports about its efficacy. It’s extremely popular. In 2025, sales of sleep supplements containing magnesium rose about 17 percent.

      It comes in many forms—magnesium glycinate, citrate, oxide, malate, threonate, taurate, chloride, and more. In other words, you don’t pop pure magnesium tablets.

      Why? Pure magnesium is a reactive metal, so supplements bind it to another compound, and that partner affects how well it’s absorbed and how it works in the body.

      Social media has promoted magnesium as a path to deeper, more restorative  sleep, but sleep scientists and medical researchers warn that the evidence doesn’t yet match the viral enthusiasm. A sleep specialist told The New York Times, “The hype is much, much further ahead than objective science.”

      Still, there is some science behind the claims.

      According to the NIH, magnesium glycinate is widely favored because the amino acid glycine attached to it has calming and relaxing benefits of its own.

      A 2025 randomized trial involving 155 adults with poor sleep found that those taking 250 mg of magnesium glycinate 30 to 60 minutes before bedtime had greater improvement in insomnia symptoms than those taking a placebo, although the benefit was modest. Another long-term study of nearly 4,000 people found that those consuming the most magnesium were 36 percent less likely to sleep fewer than seven hours and 30 percent more likely to report better-quality sleep. Because that study was observational, however, it couldn’t establish that magnesium caused the improvement.

      Magnesium glycinate and magnesium L-threonate (which I also tried) are popular for sleep because they tend to cause fewer gastrointestinal problems than citrate or oxide.

      Bottom line: For  healthy adults, magnesium at recommended doses is generally considered low-risk.

      You can get magnesium glycinate from many sources, but the product I used came from Thorne. Based on everything I’ve read, the company has a sterling reputation. Its facility is NSF (National Sanitation Foundation)-certified, which involves independent product testing, label review, facility and supplier inspections, and ongoing monitoring.

      Advertisement

      Based in Summerville, South Carolina, Thorne has collaborated with institutions such as the Mayo Clinic on wellness research. That says quite a bit. No way the Mayo Clinic would take a chance on marginal products.

      Thorne offers about 180  health and wellness products. It is known worldwide for pharmaceutical-grade, third-party-tested supplements with highly bioavailable, methylated, and chelated ingredients, free of gluten and artificial fillers. Its clinical reputation has made it a staple among medical practitioners, Olympic teams, and professional athletes in the UFC and NBA.

      Magnesium L-threonate (Magtein®) from Why Not Natural

      Magnesium L-threonate (Magtein®) was the third item on my list. Like magnesium glycinate, it’s available from several sources. Developed by researchers at MIT, it is a newer form that studies suggest may raise magnesium levels in the brain more effectively than other forms. A friend whose judgment I trust recommended it. He uses it and swears by it.

      Unlike magnesium glycinate, which is widely recommended for sleep and relaxation, Magtein® was developed to support brain health, memory, and cognitive function. In recent years, however, it has become part of many nighttime supplement regimens—often combined with L-theanine and apigenin—because many clinicians and longevity experts believe its effects on the brain may also promote healthier sleep. It has also caught on in the biohacking community.

      A 2024 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial involving 80 adults with self-reported sleep problems found that participants taking magnesium L-threonate for three weeks had significantly better objective measures of deep sleep and REM sleep (measured with an Oura Ring) than those taking a placebo. They also reported improved mood, energy, alertness, and daytime productivity.

      Why Not Natural, which sells the Magtein product I used, describes its origin story on its website: “Why Not Natural is a woman-led company borne out of our founder Kelin’s frustration with the difficulty she often experienced trying to find a good supplement. She wanted her family of five to have the best ingredients available and nothing more. And Why Not Natural wants yours to have that as well!”

      Unlike Thorne and Herbs, Etc., Why Not Natural does not manufacture its own products. It is a boutique brand that designs and formulates products in-house and outsources production to contract manufacturers.

      Advertisement

      My “clinical trial”

      Of course, I use the term “clinical trial” advisedly.

      A real clinical trial is a structured, closely monitored scientific study. I tried to be as objective as possible, but this was really a test of  sleep aids to see whether they worked for me.

      Here are the dates of each period: Baseline: Feb. 24 – April 11 (no sleep aid) Period 1: April 12 – May 11 (Magtein Magnesium L-Threonate + L-Theanine + Apigenin) Period 2: May 12 – June 11 (Magnesium Glycinate) Period 3: June 12 – July 11 (Deep Sleep Herbal Supplement) The first part of the trial, which I call the baseline, involved no sleep supplements.

      I needed data on my normal sleep patterns to compare with the supplement periods. That also meant no alcohol—no wine, beer, or any other alcoholic beverages—for the length of the trial. I also tried to keep a consistent sleep schedule, going to bed and getting up at about the same time every day. I did my best to gauge the products’ efficacy using data from my Oura Ring and my own observations. (For more information on the Oura Ring visit https://ouraring.com/)

      Essentially: How did I feel the next morning? Was I rested and ready to take on the day?

      The Oura Ring’s  sleep metrics provided the hard data: Sleep Score, Sleep Efficiency, Total Sleep Time, Deep Sleep, REM Sleep, and Sleep Latency. Unlike the Herbs, Etc. and Thorne supplements, which I took around bedtime, Magtein called for one capsule of magnesium L-threonate compound three times a day. (For some reason, the company doesn’t list the amount per capsule. The label says only that three standard-size vegetarian capsules a day provide a total of 1,000 mg of magnesium L-threonate complex–72 mg of elemental magnesium–along with 250 mg of L-theanine and 50 mg of apigenin “for enhanced relaxation.”)  

      Advertisement

      The results—a mixed bag

      Looking across all six metrics, no single supplement outperformed the baseline across the board.

      Instead, each had a distinct pattern:

      • Baseline (no supplement): Best overall  Sleep Score, longest sleep duration, and most REM sleep.
      • Period 1 (Magtein + L-Theanine + Apigenin): No clear advantage in these six measures.
      • Period 2 (Thorne Magnesium Glycinate): Most deep sleep by a noticeable margin.
      • Period 3 (Deep Sleep Herbal Supplement): Shortest time to fall asleep and a Sleep Score nearly equal to baseline.

      So how did I rate the supplements?

      Data is one thing. Perhaps more important is how I felt when I woke up.

      Although my Sleep Score was higher without supplements, I felt more rested with the Thorne Magnesium Glycinate and the Deep Sleep products. Can I explain that? No. But that was my observation.

      One thing I liked about Deep Sleep is that it comes in two forms. The soft gels are taken an hour before bedtime and again at bedtime. The tincture can be used instead: You place the drops under your tongue at bedtime. You can also use the tincture (as I did regularly) if you wake in the middle of the night and can’t drop back off to sleep. It acts faster than the soft gel, which makes it handy in those situations.

      The directions on the Thorne bottle suggest one to four capsules daily. I took one or two at bedtime. Thorne also sells magnesium glycinate as a powder, in a 7.98-ounce container with a little scoop for mixing it with water. I liked that option where you can adjust your dosage. I got creative and mixed it with water flavored with tart cherry juice, itself a popular sleep aid. The tart cherry is tasty and the trick is to limit liquid intake before bedtime.

      Advertisement

      Conclusion

      I have no doubt that both the magnesium glycinate and the Deep Sleep herbal blend “worked” when it came to getting me to sleep in a timely manner.

      I also believe it made a difference that I took the Why Not Natural Magtein + L-Theanine + Apigenin three times a day, while taking the other supplements at bedtime. No I’m not a psychologist but it seems that there was the added psychophysiological effect to swallowing a pill, drinking juice mixed with powder, or putting drops of tincture under my tongue at bedtime.

      That brings up an issue these products didn’t address: my tendency to wake in the middle of the night. These products could not mitigate this. Then again, it would be asking too much of a  sleep aid to deliver eight hours of sound sleep.

      That said, for people who have difficulty falling asleep, I can wholeheartedly recommend Deep Sleep or Thorne Magnesium Glycinate. As I mentioned, a dropper of Deep Sleep’s tincture comes in handy when you wake in the middle of the night.

      On Amazon, a 120-count container of Deep Sleep softgels costs $48.27, and the 4-ounce liquid extract (tincture) is $51.11. Thorne Magnesium Glycinate is $46 for 180 capsules. Why Not Natural’s Magnesium L-Threonate Complex (90 capsules) is $31.97.
